content.text: I'll start by looking at the flow meters in our catalog.

Here are the solar-powered units with lead times of 6 weeks or less:

| Model | Min flow (GPD) | Max flow (GPD) | Lead time | Solar | Lead time ≤ 6 wk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FM-834 (P-027) | 5 | 50 | 4 wk | Yes | Yes |
| FM-609 (P-025) | 5 | 200 | 2 wk | Yes | Yes |
| FM-694 (P-028) | 25 | 50 | 6 wk | Yes | Yes |
| FM-756 (P-021) | 25 | 400 | 4 wk | Yes | Yes |

The lowest minimum flow in the catalog is 5 GPD, on the FM-834, FM-609, FM-333, FM-977, and FM-399. At 1 GPD you would be running at a fifth of the lowest measurable flow, so readings would be unreliable or out of spec. The FM-333 and FM-977 also need grid power, and the FM-399 is battery-powered with an 8-week lead time, so they miss your other requirements as well.

- **Confirm the flow rate.** If "1 gallon per day" was a typo, or the real rate is 5 GPD or higher, the FM-609 (P-025) would be my pick. It is solar-powered, has a 2-week lead time, covers 5 to 200 GPD, and is H2S-rated. It is also rated to 5,000 psi and 400°F. The FM-834 would work for 5 to 50 GPD, but it isn't H2S-rated and costs more.
- **Look at a different measurement approach.** For a flow this low, a metering or dosing method such as a calibrated chemical injection pump with stroke counting, or a tank-level measurement, may be more practical than an inline flow meter. I can look at our injection pump options if that fits your application.

I don't want to sell you a meter that can't measure your actual flow. Let me know if the flow rate changes or if you'd like me to look at alternatives.

RECOMMENDATION: NONE

It must be rated for at least 1,000 psi. It has to handle temperatures up to 525°F. It needs to run on pneumatic power. Can you recommend something?

content.text: I'll start by listing the chemical injection pumps in the catalog.

content.content: {"category": "chemical_injection_pump", "products": [{"id": "P-001", "name": "Norvane CIP-523"}, {"id": "P-002", "name": "Norvane CIP-565"}, {"id": "P-003", "name": "Norvane CIP-480"}, {"id": "P-004", "name": "Norvane CIP-374"}, {"id": "P-005", "name": "Norvane CIP-676"}, {"id": "P-006", "name": "Norvane CIP-696"}, {"id": "P-007", "name": "Norvane CIP-122"}, {"id": "P-008", "name": "Norvane CIP-809"}, {"id": "P-009", "name": "Norvane CIP-297"}, {"id": "P-010", "name": "Norvane CIP-832"}]}

content.text: I'll pull the specs for all of them.

I checked all ten chemical injection pumps in the catalog against your four requirements: at least 1,000 psi, 525°F, pneumatic power, and delivery within 14 weeks. None of them meets all four, so I can't recommend one.

The 525°F temperature is what rules them out. The highest temperature rating in the catalog is 500°F, and nothing is rated above that.

Of the pneumatic pumps, these meet everything except the temperature:

| Pump | Max temp | Max pressure | Flow (gpd) | Lead time | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **CIP-565 (P-002)** | 500°F | 1,500 psi | 10–100 | 12 weeks | $8,600 |
| **CIP-374 (P-004)** | 500°F | 7,500 psi | 10–200 | 8 weeks | $13,400 |

The other pneumatic pumps fall further short on temperature:
- CIP-523 (P-001): 250°F
- CIP-696 (P-006): 400°F
- CIP-832 (P-010): 400°F

The remaining pumps don't run on pneumatic power: P-003, P-007, P-008 and P-009 are solar, and P-005 is electric.

The CIP-565 and CIP-374 are each 25°F under your spec. If your 525°F figure is a worst-case or transient peak rather than sustained operating temperature, either could work. That would need to be confirmed against the actual process conditions and the manufacturer's tolerances. If 525°F is a continuous operating temperature, neither is suitable.

If a 500°F rating is acceptable, I'd lean toward the CIP-374. It has more pressure headroom, a wider flow range and a shorter lead time, but it costs more. The CIP-565 is cheaper and still meets your 14-week window at 12 weeks, as long as you don't need the extra pressure or flow capacity.

Let me know if the temperature requirement can be relaxed or if you'd like me to look at other options.

RECOMMENDATION: NONE

Fluid temperature can reach 525°F. We need it delivered within 7 weeks. Our target rate is 30 gal/day. Working pressure is 4,000 psi, so it needs a rating at least that high. What would you recommend?

content.text: I'll start by looking at the chemical injection pumps in our catalog.

content.text: Let me pull the specs on all of them.

I checked all 10 chemical injection pumps against your requirements (solar power, 525°F, 4,000 psi, 30 gal/day, delivery within 7 weeks). None of them meets all of them, so I can't recommend one.

The solar-powered units are the only ones that fit your power constraint:

| Model | Power | Max temp | Max pressure | Flow range | Lead time | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CIP-809 (P-008) | Solar | 500°F | 5,000 psi | 1-50 gpd | 6 wks | Fails on temperature (500°F vs. 525°F) |

| CIP-480 (P-003) | Solar | 400°F | 1,500 psi | 10-800 gpd | 8 wks | Fails on temperature, pressure and lead time |

No pump in the catalog is rated for 525°F. The highest rating is 500°F, on the CIP-809, CIP-565 and CIP-374. The CIP-565 and CIP-374 are also pneumatic, not solar.

The CIP-809 is the closest fit. It meets the solar, pressure (5,000 psi vs. 4,000 psi), flow (30 gpd is within 1-50) and lead time (6 weeks) requirements. It falls 25°F short of your peak fluid temperature. I wouldn't put it in service at 525°F, because running beyond the rated temperature risks seal and component failure.

Here are some options:
- **Confirm the peak temperature.** If 525°F is a worst-case spike and normal operation stays at or below 500°F, you could use the CIP-809 with appropriate safeguards, such as cooling or a standoff arrangement. Your engineering team would need to approve that.
- **Add thermal mitigation.** Cooling or isolating the pump from the hot fluid could bring the temperature at the pump within its rating.
- **Look at a different power source.** If a compressed gas supply or grid power could be added, the CIP-374 (500°F, 7,500 psi, pneumatic, 8 weeks) is another option. It would still be 25°F short and wouldn't meet the 7-week window.

If you can tell me whether the 525°F figure is a sustained or peak temperature, I can help work out the next step.

RECOMMENDATION: NONE

- **CIP-696 (P-006):** It is H2S rated and handles 400°F, but its 200 GPD maximum is below your 230 GPD.
